verdict.headline: The ten-year Treasury yield touched 5% for the first time since 2023 and closed below it
verdict.label: Ten-year reached 5.01% intraday, its first 5% print since 2023, and was bought back under the level; thirty-year 5.353%. S&P 500 -0.48% to 7,619.98, Nasdaq -0.56% to 26,186.41, Dow -0.29% to 52,421.20, Russell -0.40% to 2,892.24. Brent ran above $109 intraday to about $108.15 and WTI to $102.64 with no Hormuz meeting scheduled. Cybersecurity rose 15% against Marvell -6.00% and Nvidia -2.91%; Kospi -3.26%, SoftBank -10%. Gold -1.25% to $4,284.48, DXY +0.32% to 99.44, September 16 hike priced near 87%
verdict.rationale_short:
The ten-year Treasury yield reached 5.01% on Monday, its first print at that level since 2023, before buyers took it back under 5% into the close. What moved it was crude and government borrowing rather than the Federal Reserve. Brent ran to a session high above $109 and traded near $108.15, with WTI near $102.64, after Oman's postponed Iran-Gulf talks left Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline workaround shut from the September 10-11 drone strikes. Wednesday's quarter-point hike was already priced near 87% when the session opened, and the committee is in blackout, so no policy signal was available to produce the move. The level was reached and rejected inside one session, which says demand exists at 5% but not below it.

The hike has stopped being the question. Goldman Sachs abandoned its call for no change and now expects a 25 bp increase, with chief US economist David Mericle writing that the committee "will be reluctant to surprise" a market pricing one at roughly 90% — a forecast changed because the market priced it is an argument that the decision itself carries almost no information. The bank still does not carry further increases after September in its base case, which is a testable disagreement with any dot plot showing two. That places the entire information content of Wednesday in the Summary of Economic Projections rather than in the rate.

Equities absorbed the rates move but not evenly. The S&P 500 fell 0.48% to 7,619.98 and the Nasdaq Composite 0.56% to 26,186.41, well off the intraday low, against Nasdaq-100 futures that had been down 1.5% before the open. Underneath, money rotated rather than left: CrowdStrike and Zscaler rose 15% and Palo Alto Networks 13% in midday trade, holding their premarket gains rather than fading them, while Marvell fell 6.00% to $221.94, Nvidia 2.91% to $211.94, and Intel and AMD 4% each. Communication services gained 2.79% and health care 1.35% while technology fell 1.67%. The same catalyst cost far more abroad: the Kospi lost 3.26% with SK Hynix off more than 6%, and SoftBank fell 10% in Tokyo, which locates the exposure in the hardware supply chain rather than in US equities broadly.

Two dislocations cut against the simple reading. Energy fell 0.94% and utilities 1.34% on a day crude gained 2%, which points at the AI power-demand trade rather than at the barrel, and reverses XLE's 1.2% premarket bid. And gold fell 1.25% to $4,284.48 with silver down 2.14% while the dollar index rose 0.32% to 99.44 — metals sold as the war premium in crude widened, which reads as a real-rate and dollar repricing rather than the safety bid a Gulf escalation would normally produce. Separately, The Information identified Anthropic as the customer behind a six-year, $13.7 billion compute contract disclosed in an August filing, sending Rum Group up about 10% while CoreWeave and Nebius each fell 9%: the lab arguing publicly for slower capability growth signed one of the year's largest compute commitments, and the rented-compute group traded it as a share shift rather than as new demand.

The levels that would change the picture: a ten-year close above 5.00%, as distinct from today's intraday touch, would price a hike that has not settled the inflation question, while a retreat under 4.90% after Wednesday would say the market read the move as the end of the cycle. A WTI settle under $100 would say the war premium is deflating with no diplomacy behind it; above $105 puts a second month of energy pass-through into the data the committee sees after the decision. Neither has happened yet.
verdict.lede_short: The ten-year Treasury yield hit 5.01% on Monday, its first 5% print since 2023, then was bought back under the level — moved by crude above $109 and Treasury supply, not by a Fed hike already priced near 87%. Equities absorbed it unevenly: the S&P 500 fell 0.48% while cybersecurity rose 15% against Marvell's 6% decline and a 3.26% drop in Korea. A close above 5.00% around Wednesday's dot plot would confirm the level; under 4.90% would say the market read the hike as the cycle's end.

supporting_data.label: The ten-year Treasury yield rose almost five basis points to as high as 5.01%, its first touch of 5% since 2023, then erased the increase as buyers emerged, with the thirty-year at 5.353% — the level was reached and rejected inside one session, which says demand exists at 5% but not below it

Brent climbed past $109 intraday to trade near $108.15 and WTI near $102.64, after Oman postponed the Iran-Gulf talks on a temporary Hormuz shipping lane and Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline stayed shut from the September 10-11 drone strikes — the second consecutive session in which the energy input rather than the policy input set the long end

Goldman Sachs abandoned its call for no change and now expects a 25 bp hike Wednesday, with chief US economist David Mericle writing the committee "will be reluctant to surprise" a market pricing one near 90%, while the bank still carries no further increases after September — a forecast changed because the market priced it argues the decision carries almost no information and the projections carry all of it

The Information identified Anthropic as the customer behind Rum Group's six-year, $13.7 billion compute contract for a data center under construction in Georgia, sending the stock up about 10% while CoreWeave fell 9% to $81.25 and Nebius 9% to $205.28 — the lab arguing publicly for slower capability growth signed one of the year's largest compute commitments, and rented-compute peers traded it as a share shift rather than as new demand

Gold fell 1.25% to $4,284.48 and silver 2.14% to $63.22 while the dollar index rose 0.32% to 99.44 — metals sold on a day the war premium in crude widened, which reads as a real-rate and dollar repricing rather than the safety bid a Gulf escalation would normally produce

South Korea's Kospi fell 3.26% to 6,684.37 with SK Hynix down more than 6% and Samsung more than 4%, and SoftBank lost 10% in Tokyo — the same AI-slowdown catalyst cost Seoul nearly seven times what it cost the S&P 500, locating the exposure in the hardware supply chain rather than in US equities broadly

watchlist_mentions.note: Closed down 2.91% at $211.94, a smaller decline than Marvell's 6.00% or the 4% in Intel and AMD, and the dispersion held the shape it had premarket. The market is marking down the duration of the capex cycle, which reaches merchant silicon and memory before it reaches the name carrying the order book. No guidance changed.

Fell 6.00% to $221.94, the worst of the large-cap US semis, with SK Hynix off more than 6% in Seoul on the same catalyst. Custom-silicon and memory revenue is tied to the next build rather than the installed base, which is why a statement about the pace of frontier development prices here first.

Rose 15% with Zscaler also 15% and Palo Alto Networks 13% in midday trade, holding and extending premarket gains rather than fading them. A one-day narrative bid normally decays through the session; this one did not, which is the strongest available evidence that the AI-risk trade is being underwritten rather than traded.

WTI traded near $102.64 against Friday's $100.05 settle, with Brent above $109 intraday. No replacement date exists for the postponed Iran-Gulf Hormuz meeting and the Saudi East-West pipeline is still shut, so nothing scheduled before the FOMC can resolve the premium. XLE closed down 0.94% on the same session.

Touched 5.01% intraday, the first 5% print since 2023, and was bought back under the level with the thirty-year at 5.353%, nine basis points below the 2007 peak of 5.44%. The rejection came from buyers rather than from a policy signal, with the committee in blackout. A close above 5.00% around Wednesday's projections would confirm the level.

trade_setups.thesis: The yield reached 5.01% and was rejected by buyers appearing rather than by anything changing in the inputs behind it. Crude is above $108, the Oman meeting has no date, Treasury supply across a $32 trillion market is unchanged, and the committee is in blackout. What is forming is a test of whether 5% is a ceiling that absorbed a genuine energy and supply shock or a waypoint that positioning defended for one session. The counter-evidence to a durable break is that the hike is priced at roughly 87% and Goldman, having just flipped to a hike, still carries none after September.
trade_setups.entry: 5.00% on the ten-year is the level that defines it, with 4.90% below and the thirty-year's 5.44% 2007 peak above; today's 5.01% high and roughly 4.99% close are the reference prints.
trade_setups.invalidation: A close above 5.00% in the two sessions around Wednesday's projections would say the rejection was positioning; a retreat under 4.90% after the decision would say the market read the hike as the end of the cycle.
trade_setups.horizon: Wednesday September 16 into the following week

trade_setups.asset: Anthropic's listing and the AI-slowdown argument
trade_setups.thesis: The public S-1 is expected in late September ahead of a mid-October roadshow, supporting a listing valued at up to $2 trillion with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan leading — weeks after the company's chief executive argued publicly for slowing the rate at which model capabilities improve. The risk-factor section is the first document in which that argument has to be written down in a form investors price. The same session showed the argument and the spending are not yet in conflict: the company was identified as the customer behind a six-year, $13.7 billion compute contract.
trade_setups.entry: The S-1 filing date and the risk-factor language are the observables; the reference prints are semis down 3-6% and cybersecurity up 13-15% on the day the argument was first traded.
trade_setups.invalidation: An S-1 that treats capability pacing as a routine regulatory risk rather than a business constraint, or a further compute commitment of comparable size, would say the market overpriced the statement.

trade_setups.thesis: XLE went from up 1.2% premarket to down 0.94% at the close while Brent held above $108, and utilities fell 1.34% on the same session. Crude and the equities that produce and power its economy separated, with the AI power-demand unwind the available explanation and Siemens Energy's 8.04% decline in Frankfurt the read-across. Against that, energy remains the year's best-performing S&P sector and one session is not a trend; what is forming is a question about whether the sector is now valued on electricity demand rather than on the oil price.
trade_setups.entry: The gap itself is the observable: Brent above $108 with XLE negative. Utilities and independent power names are where the AI-demand leg shows first.
trade_setups.invalidation: XLE rising with crude through a week that still has no Hormuz date would say Monday was a one-session rotation artifact rather than a change in what the sector is priced on.
